arguments.objective: Write a rigorous technical deep-dive covering SSA construction and alias analysis, with at least 3 named mechanisms each, in real depth.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical write-up with two sections:

SECTION 1: SSA CONSTRUCTION
Cover at least three specific named mechanisms in depth, using precise standard terminology. Required candidates to cover (pick at least 3, more is fine):
- Dominance frontier-based phi insertion (Cytron et al. algorithm): dominator tree construction, iterated dominance frontier, minimal/pruned SSA
- Sparse Simple Linear-time (Braun et al.) SSA construction algorithm with incomplete CFGs, local value numbering, and SSA construction without dominance frontiers
- SSA destruction / out-of-SSA translation (phi-node elimination, parallel copy sequentialization, dealing with the lost-copy and swap problems)
- Semi-pruned SSA, pruned SSA via liveness
- Memory SSA / Array SSA extensions
Explain each mechanism's algorithmic steps, complexity, and tradeoffs (e.g., Cytron vs Braun approach for compile-time speed vs incremental updates).

SECTION 2: ALIAS ANALYSIS
Cover at least three specific named mechanisms in depth:
- Andersen's points-to analysis (inclusion-based, subset constraints, cubic complexity)
- Steensgaard's points-to analysis (unification-based, near-linear complexity, equality constraints)
- Type-based alias analysis (TBAA) as used in C/C++ compilers (strict aliasing rules)
- Flow-sensitive vs flow-insensitive alias analysis distinctions
- Shape analysis / field-sensitive analysis
- Anderson-style context-sensitivity (k-CFA) for interprocedural alias analysis
Discuss precision/scalability tradeoffs, how these integrate into optimizing compilers (e.g., LLVM's AliasAnalysis infrastructure, basicaa, scev-aa, tbaa metadata).

Be exhaustive and precise. Use correct standard terminology throughout. Target length: detailed enough to serve as a technical reference, roughly 600-900 words per section.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous technical deep-dive covering register allocation and inlining, with at least 3 named mechanisms each, in real depth.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical write-up with two sections:

SECTION 1: REGISTER ALLOCATION
Cover at least three specific named mechanisms in depth, using precise standard terminology. Required candidates to cover (pick at least 3, more is fine):
- Graph coloring register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs algorithm): interference graph construction, simplify/spill worklist, optimistic coloring, coalescing (conservative/Briggs coalescing vs Iterated Register Coalescing by George/Appel)
- Linear scan register allocation: live interval computation, active/inactive interval sets, spill heuristics, use in JIT compilers (e.g., V8, early LLVM)
- SSA-based register allocation (Hack/Goos/Palsberg): chordal interference graphs from SSA form, simplifying coloring via SSA's chordality property
- Puzzle-solving / PBQP (Partitioned Boolean Quadratic Programming) register allocation
- Spill code generation and rematerialization
- Live range splitting
Discuss complexity, precision, and compile-time tradeoffs, and where each is used in real compilers (GCC, LLVM, JVM HotSpot, V8).

SECTION 2: INLINING
Cover at least three specific named mechanisms in depth:
- Cost-benefit heuristic inlining (size/speed cost models, threshold-based decisions as in GCC/LLVM inline cost analysis)
- Profile-guided inlining (hot/cold splitting using PGO data)
- Partial inlining
- Inlining with devirtualization (speculative inlining with guards, inline caches as in JIT compilers like V8/HotSpot)
- Recursive/self-recursive inlining limits and bottom-up vs top-down inlining order (call graph SCC-based inlining)
- Cross-module / link-time inlining (LTO-based inlining)
Discuss how each integrates into the broader pipeline and its tradeoffs regarding code size, compile time, and runtime performance.

Be exhaustive and precise. Target length: roughly 600-900 words per section.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous technical deep-dive covering escape analysis and loop vectorization, with at least 3 named mechanisms each, in real depth.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical write-up with two sections:

SECTION 1: ESCAPE ANALYSIS
Cover at least three specific named mechanisms in depth, using precise standard terminology. Candidates to cover:
- Connection graph / points-to based escape analysis (as in the Choi/Gupta/Sarkar algorithm used in JVM/HotSpot) - escape states (NoEscape, ArgEscape, GlobalEscape)
- Stack allocation / scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA) enabled by escape analysis
- Lock elision / synchronization elimination enabled by escape analysis (biased locking removal)
- Partial escape analysis (as used in Graal compiler) with deoptimization-based materialization
- Allocation sinking
- Flow-sensitive vs flow-insensitive escape analysis
Discuss how these integrate into JIT compilers (HotSpot C2, Graal) and static compilers (Go compiler's escape analysis for heap vs stack allocation decisions).

SECTION 2: LOOP VECTORIZATION
Cover at least three specific named mechanisms in depth:
- Loop-level (outer-loop) vectorization vs SLP (Superword Level Parallelism) vectorization
- Data dependence analysis for vectorization (distance/direction vectors, GCD test, Banerjee test)
- Vectorization legality via loop-carried dependence checking, and alignment analysis
- Strip mining / loop sectioning for fitting vector widths
- Predicated/masked vectorization for handling control flow (if-conversion)
- Cost modeling for vectorization decisions (interleaving factor, vector width selection, as in LLVM's LoopVectorize pass)
- Reduction vectorization (handling associative/commutative reduction idioms)
Discuss real implementations (LLVM LoopVectorizer and SLPVectorizer, GCC's tree-vectorizer) and tradeoffs.

Be exhaustive and precise. Target length: roughly 600-900 words per section.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous technical deep-dive covering instruction scheduling and loop optimizations, with at least 3 named mechanisms each, in real depth.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical write-up with two sections:

SECTION 1: INSTRUCTION SCHEDULING
Cover at least three specific named mechanisms in depth, using precise standard terminology. Candidates to cover:
- List scheduling (priority-based scheduling over a data dependence DAG, critical path heuristics)
- Local scheduling vs global scheduling (basic block vs trace/superblock scheduling)
- Trace scheduling (Fisher's algorithm) for VLIW/ILP exploitation across branches, including compensation code
- Software pipelining (modulo scheduling), including the concept of minimum initiation interval (MII) determination via resource and recurrence constraints
- List scheduling with register pressure sensitivity (combining scheduling with register allocation concerns)
- Sentinel/hazard-aware scheduling for pipeline hazards and latency hiding
Discuss real compiler implementations (LLVM's MachineScheduler, GCC's haifa-sched, Itanium/VLIW software pipelining compilers).

SECTION 2: LOOP OPTIMIZATIONS
Cover at least three specific named mechanisms in depth (note: do not re-cover vectorization in depth here, focus on other loop transforms):
- Loop-invariant code motion (LICM), including speculative/sinking variants
- Loop unrolling (full vs partial) and unroll-and-jam
- Loop fusion and loop fission/distribution
- Loop interchange (for locality/parallelism, legality via dependence direction vectors)
- Loop tiling/blocking for cache locality
- Induction variable simplification / strength reduction (linear IV recognition, SCEV - scalar evolution analysis as in LLVM)
- Loop unswitching
Discuss legality conditions (dependence analysis), profitability heuristics, and real implementations.

Be exhaustive and precise. Target length: roughly 600-900 words per section.
